To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the WEP initialization vector (IV) is reused too often; (2) the IV is not randomized; and (3) the RC4 keystream is not properly protected.

(1) WEP is vulnerable to a known plaintext attack, which can be used to decrypt all past and future packets; (2) WEP is susceptible to a key-recovery attack that can be performed in real-time, and which can recover the key in less than 15 minutes on a 11-Mbps 802.11 network; (3) WEP is subject to a related-key attack; and (4) WEP is not a secure authentication protocol.

WEP is not collision resistant, and therefore can be broken in a matter of seconds using a simple brute-force attack; WEP is vulnerable to a chosen plaintext attack that can be carried out in under a minute; the IV space is exhausted in a matter of hours, allowing an adversary to decrypt any packet in a matter of minutes; the IV space exhaustion attack is not only a passive attack but can be carried out as a denial of service attack.
